title: An ancient hymn says even the creator may not know how creation began
body: The Nasadiya Sukta is hymn 129 of the tenth book of the Rigveda, the oldest of the Vedic texts. It opens by saying that in the beginning there was neither non-existence nor existence, no air and no sky beyond, and asks: what covered it, where was it, in whose keeping? It names desire as the first seed, born of the mind, then pulls back: the gods came after creation, so who can know? The final verse turns to the creator ‘who surveys it all from highest heaven’: **‘he knows — or maybe even he does not know’**. Some readers see one of the earliest written examples of sceptical inquiry.

slides.text: Whence all creation had its origin, the creator, whether he fashioned it or whether he did not, the creator, who surveys it all from highest heaven, he knows — or maybe even he does not know.
slides.attribution: Rigveda 10.129, verse 7, translated by A. L. Basham

slides.heading: The hymn’s moves
items: Before anything: neither existence nor non-existence, no air, no sky
Darkness wrapped in darkness; then the One arose
Desire descends: the first seed, born of the mind
But who knows? The gods came after creation

slides.heading: Doubt in a holy book
slides.text: The hymn sits inside a sacred collection, yet it ends in a question rather than a doctrine. Some read it as one of the earliest accounts of sceptical inquiry and agnosticism; others as a reminder that the origin of everything lies beyond what minds can reach.

slides.question: According to the hymn, when did the gods appear?
options: The hymn says they never did
slides.explanation: ‘The gods themselves are later than creation, so who knows truly whence it has arisen?’ That is why the hymn says even the gods cannot answer.
